- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.6) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slightly.
- When sentiment is negative (≤0.2) or volatile, model often underestimates; adjust upward, especially if recent price is falling.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >10% from prior peak), model frequently overshoots; cap forecast at 1.5x prior peak or use moving average to smooth.
- If model forecast is >10% above recent 7-day average, consider mean reversion bias; reduce by 10–20% unless sentiment strongly supports.
- For 30-day horizon, model often lags 1–2 days behind true trend; add 1–2% lagged momentum to forecast if sentiment is trending.
- If sentiment history shows repeated “reversal” patterns (e.g., +0.3 → -0.3 → +0.3), model tends to mispredict direction; use sentiment-weighted moving average for direction.
- When sentiment is high but price is falling, model often ignores sentiment; force a slight downward bias to align with sentiment.
- If model forecast is consistently below true outcome by 2–3% over 3–5 days, consider sentiment-driven “rebound” rule: add 0.5–1.0% to forecast if sentiment >0.7.
